items.title: 67460_Sammy Price oral history interview
items.q: He said, 'No matter what you see me do, or what I do, don't you worry.' Do you know that he called at least a hundred piano players to play with me? James P. Johnson, Willie the Lion Smith, Donald Lambert , Meade Lux Lewis, Pete Johnson, da, da and da.

ctx.x: It was a very interesting training ground. It was like a Who's Who in America, you know, in black America because if they were anybody, from Georgie Williams and Bessie Brown to Bert Williams to Ma Rainey to Trixie Smith to...well, Ella wasn't around in those days, you know...you know this TOBA was way before. And Joe Bright, and you had...and most of these towns that they played were towns in the Southwest, starting, for example...they had like a circuit, and you'd start in...occasionally in Chicago, but mostly…

some money you'd say, 'Now, when you get down in Shreveport, give this to my aunt and stay with her that week.' And maybe coming from the other way, Louisville, you come back down to Winston-Salem and back down and all until you get to Shreveport and you give the money to the parent or the mother of the friend, and so forth. So, I think that, that one thing that that thing taught you was fidelity, friendship and respect and recognition. Now we don't practice that all the time, that's an important fact. For…

have been like that with musicians, that I would share what I have, like I knew how to...well, I won't say I knew how to get money from women, but I knew...well, you know, women liked me and they would want to do me favors, and if some guy...you understand, Dan, wasn't doing too well, he could always come to me. That guy was here, right here. One time I owed my rent...my rent was a thousand dollars and his rent was a hundred and I had a hundred dollars. And you know what I did? I gave it to him. He paid his rent.…

items.title: 67460_Sammy Price oral history interview
items.q: So we became very, very close.

ctx.x: So, that's how I made it in New York City. And plus the fact that I usually try to help people. Then you know, you remember Adam Clayton Powell. The first political advisor he had was my uncle and this is how I happened to go into the political arena. I had a license on Broadway as a booking agent. Legitimate booking agent. Not, you know, sub-booking for somebody or, you know, I'm waiting for it to be approved.
I had an office at 1674 Broadway. That's where I gave Willie 'the Lion' and James P. Johnson an office just to come and play...

Adam Clayton Powell...this was during the early days before he, you know, went into politics proper...There was a man in central Harlem named Joseph E. Ford. Joe Ford was my uncle. And, aside from having all these other good things happen to me, you know, getting jobs and making records and broadening my acquaintance with a lot of people...then when I find Uncle Joe, I find him in an NAACP boat ride I believe it was. They were giving an NAACP boat ride. And this man was standing down at 125th Street on the pier,…
